{{nihongo|'''Nunakuma Shrine'''|沼名前神社}} is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|abstract|Q845945|ar|جينجا|arz|ضريح شنتو|bcl|Shinto shrine|ca|Jinja|cs|Šintoistická svatyně|da|Shinto-tempel|de|Shintō-Schrein|el|Σιντοϊστικό Ιερό|eo|Ŝintoa sanktejo|es|Jinja|eu|Jinja|fa|معبد شینتویی|fi|Šintolainen pyhäkkö|fr|Sanctuaire shinto|hi|शिंतो मंदिर|hr|Šintoistički hram|hu|Sintó szentély|id|Jinja|it|Jinja|ja|神社|ka|ძინძია|ko|신사 (신토)|lb|Shintō-Schräin|mr|शिंतो मंदिर|nl|Jinja (heiligdom)|no|Jinja|or|ଜିଞ୍ଜା|pl|Jinja|pt|Templo xintoísta|ru|Дзиндзя|sc|Jinja|simple|Shinto shrine|sl|Šintoistično svetišče|sr|Шинтоистички храм|sv|Jinja|th|ศาลเจ้าชินโต|tok|tomo sewi pi nasin sewi Sinto|tr|Şinto tapınağı|uk|Святилище (синто)|uz|Dzindzya|vi|Thần xã|wuu|神社|zh|神社|zh_yue|神社|qid=Q845945}} located in Tomo-chō Ushiroji, {{ill|Fukuyama, Hiroshima|Q661038|qid=Q661038}}, {{ill|Hiroshima Prefecture|Q617375|qid=Q617375}}. It is a {{ill|Shikinaisha|fr|Shikinaisha|zh|式內社|qid=Q134917286|lt=Shikinaisha}}, and under the former {{ill|Q712534|lt=Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines}}, it was ranked as a {{ill|Q712534|lt=Kanpei-shōsha}}. Today, it is listed as a {{ill|Beppyo shrine|ja|別表神社|mr|बेप्प्यो तीर्थ|simple|Beppyo shrine|zh|別表神社|qid=Q10898274}} under the {{ill|Association of Shinto Shrines|Q908077|qid=Q908077}}. {{nihongo|'''Nunakuma Shrine'''|沼名前神社}} is a [[shinto shrine]] in the [[Engishiki Jinmyōchō]]. It is located in [[Bingo Province]].

In addition to the name “Tomo Gion-gū,” it is also commonly called “Gion-san” or “Ogion-san.”

== Enshrined deities ==
The shrine enshrines the following two deities<ref>The description of the enshrined deities is based on the [http://tomo-gionsan.com/yuisyo.shtml History] (official website).</ref>.
; Principal deity
:* {{ill|Watatsumi|abstract|Q1474187|az|Vatatsumi|de|Watatsumi|es|Watatsumi|fa|واتاتسومی|fr|Watatsumi|hu|Vatacumi|ja|ワタツミ|ko|와타쓰미|mni|ꯋꯇꯠꯁꯨꯃꯤ|pl|Watatsumi|ru|Ватацуми|simple|Watatsumi|uk|Вататсумі|zh|綿津見|qid=Q1474187|lt=Ōwatatsumi-no-Mikoto}} – Formerly the enshrined deity of Watasu Shrine.
; Associated deity
:* {{ill|Susanoo-no-Mikoto|Q272993|qid=Q272993|lt=Susanoo-no-Mikoto}} – Formerly the enshrined deity of Tomo Gion-gū.

== History ==
The present Nunakuma Shrine was formed in the {{ill|Meiji era|Q3125096|qid=Q3125096}} by the merger of '''Watasu Shrine''' and '''Tomo Gion-gū''', and was renamed “Nunakuma Shrine” in accordance with the listing in the {{ill|Engishiki|Q1342448|qid=Q1342448}} {{ill|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|abstract|Q11064932|fr|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|ja|延喜式神名帳|simple|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|zh|延喜式神名帳|qid=Q11064932|lt=Register of Deities}}<ref name="地名">“Place Names of Hiroshima Prefecture,” entry on Nunakuma Shrine.</ref>. The shrine maintains that Watasu Shrine was the shrine listed in the Engishiki and that it continues to the present day<ref name="由緒"/>. The current two enshrined deities ({{ill|Watatsumi|abstract|Q1474187|az|Vatatsumi|de|Watatsumi|es|Watatsumi|fa|واتاتسومی|fr|Watatsumi|hu|Vatacumi|ja|ワタツミ|ko|와타쓰미|mni|ꯋꯇꯠꯁꯨꯃꯤ|pl|Watatsumi|ru|Ватацуми|simple|Watatsumi|uk|Вататсумі|zh|綿津見|qid=Q1474187|lt=Ōwatatsumi-no-Mikoto}} and {{ill|Susanoo-no-Mikoto|Q272993|qid=Q272993|lt=Susanoo-no-Mikoto}}) were formerly the deities of the respective shrines prior to the merger<ref name="由緒">[http://tomo-gionsan.com/yuisyo.shtml History] (official website).</ref>.

== Watasu Shrine ==
[[File:Nunakuma-jinja Watasu-sha-2.jpg|thumb|200px|right|{{center|Watasu Shrine}}{{small|Former shrine building prior to enshrinement in the main hall.}}]]
According to shrine tradition, the founding of Watasu Shrine (now Nunakuma Shrine) dates to Year 2 of Emperor {{ill|Emperor Chūai|Q179971|qid=Q179971}}, when {{ill|Empress Jingū|Q232803|qid=Q232803}} prayed for safe sea passage by enshrining Watatsumi-no-Mikoto on a sacred stone at this site while heading westward<ref name="由緒"/>. Upon her return, she offered a “Izuno Takatomo” (a type of bow accessory; {{ill|tomo|Q11663860|qid=Q11663860}} refers to one such implement), from which the place name “Tomo” is said to have originated<ref name="由緒"/>.

In the mid-{{ill|Heian period|Q193292|qid=Q193292}}, the {{ill|Engishiki|Q1342448|qid=Q1342448}} {{ill|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|abstract|Q11064932|fr|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|ja|延喜式神名帳|simple|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|zh|延喜式神名帳|qid=Q11064932|lt=Register of Deities}} lists a {{ill|Shikinaisha|fr|Shikinaisha|zh|式內社|qid=Q134917286|lt=Shikinaisha}} named “Nunakuma Shrine” in {{ill|Bingo Province|Q1049113|qid=Q1049113}}, {{ill|Numakuma District, Hiroshima|Q7069042|qid=Q7069042}}. The reading is given as either “Nunasaki” or “Nunakuma.” Later, the location of this shrine became unknown<ref name="地名"/>. In early modern scholarship, it is identified with Watasu Shrine, though whether it was located in Tomo remains unclear<ref name="地名"/>.

In the early modern period, Watasu Shrine is said to have enshrined Sarutahiko-no-Kami and Funadama-no-Mikoto (also called Funatama-no-Mikoto)<ref name="地名"/>. It is also said to have originally been located either in Ushiroji-Hiramura or Tomo-no-Sekimachi, and to have been relocated to its present site as a subsidiary shrine of the Gion Shrine during the {{ill|Keichō|ca|Keichō|es|Keichō|fa|کیچو (دوره)|fr|Ère Keichō|id|Keichō|it|Keichō|ja|慶長|ko|게이초|ru|Кэйтё|simple|Keichō|sr|Кеичо|sv|Keichō|th|เคโช|tr|Keichō|uk|Кейтьо|zh|慶長|qid=Q1328185}} era ({{ill|1596|ab|1596|af|1596|als|1596|am|1596 እ.ኤ.አ.|an|1596|ar|1596|ary|1596|arz|1596|ast|1596|avk|1596|az|1596|azb|۱۵۹۶ (میلادی)|bar|1596|bcl|1596|be|1596|be_x_old|1596|bg|1596|bn|১৫৯৬|bpy|মারি ১৫৯৬|br|1596|bs|1596.|ca|1596|cdo|1596 nièng|ce|1596 шо|ceb|1596|ckb|١٥٩٦|crh|1596|cs|1596|cv|1596|cy|1596|da|1596|de|1596|diq|1596|el|1596|eml|1596|eo|1596|es|1596|et|1596|eu|1596|fa|۱۵۹۶ (میلادی)|fi|1596|fo|1596|fr|1596|frr|1596|fur|1596|fy|1596|ga|1596|gan|1596年|gcr|1596|gd|1596|gl|1596|gv|1596|he|1596|hi|१५९६|hif|1596|hr|1596.|ht|1596 (almanak gregoryen)|hu|1596|hy|1596|hyw|1596 թուական|ia|1596|id|1596|ilo|1596|io|1596|is|1596|it|1596|ja|1596年|jv|1596|ka|1596|kaa|1596|kk|1596 жыл|ko|1596년|krc|1596 джыл|la|1596|lb|1596|lij|1596|lmo|1596|lt|1596 m.|lv|1596. gads|mai|१५९६|map_bms|1596|mdf|1596|mg|1596|mhr|1596|mi|1596|mk|1596|mr|इ.स. १५९६|mrj|1596 и|ms|1596|my|၁၅၉၆|mzn|۱۵۹۶|nah|1596|nap|1596|nds|1596|new|सन् १५९६|nl|1596|nn|1596|no|1596|nrm|1596|nso|1596|oc|1596|olo|1596|or|୧୫୯୬|os|1596-æм аз|pl|1596|pnb|1596|pt|1596|qu|1596|ro|1596|ru|1596 год|rue|1596|sa|१५९६|sah|1596 сыл|sc|1596|scn|1596|sd|1596ع|se|1596|sh|1596.|shn|1596|simple|1596|sk|1596|sl|1596|smn|1596|sq|1596|sr|1596|su|1596|sv|1596|sw|1596|ta|1596|tg|Соли 1596|th|พ.ศ. 2139|tk|1596|tl|1596|tly|1596|tr|1596|tt|1596 ел|uk|1596|ur|1596ء|uz|1596|vec|1596|vi|1596|vls|1596|wa|1596|war|1596|wuu|1596年|xmf|1596|yi|1596|zea|1596|zh|1596年|zh_min_nan|1596 nî|zh_yue|1596年|qid=Q6785}}–{{ill|1615|Q6784|qid=Q6784}})<ref name="地名"/>. During the {{ill|Meireki|Q1192766|qid=Q1192766}} era ({{ill|1655|Q6975|qid=Q6975}}–{{ill|1658|Q6991|qid=Q6991}}), the shrine buildings were rebuilt by the domain lord {{ill|Mizuno Katsusada|Q10565395|qid=Q10565395}}<ref name="地名"/><ref>“Gods of Japan” states that Watasu Shrine was originally in Nishi-machi, Tomo, but after being destroyed by fire in Keichō 4 (1599), it was relocated to Asadani in Ushiroji Village, and later moved to the precincts of the Gion Shrine when it was rebuilt in Jōkyō 2 (1674).</ref>.

== Tomo Gion-gū ==
According to the shrine, the founding date of Tomo Gion-gū is unknown<ref name="由緒"/>. It is variously said to have been founded during the {{ill|Tenchō|Q1373138|qid=Q1373138}} era ({{ill|824|Q30353|qid=Q30353}}–{{ill|834|Q30381|qid=Q30381}}) or established by invitation during the {{ill|Hōgen (era)|Q1193898|qid=Q1193898}} era ({{ill|1156|Q19653|qid=Q19653}}–{{ill|1159|Q19659|qid=Q19659}})<ref name="地名"/>.

The enshrined deity was, as now, {{ill|Susanoo-no-Mikoto|Q272993|qid=Q272993|lt=Susanoo-no-Mikoto}}<ref name="地名"/>. The shrine was originally located in Sekimachi, Tomo, but was destroyed by fire in {{ill|Keichō|ca|Keichō|es|Keichō|fa|کیچو (دوره)|fr|Ère Keichō|id|Keichō|it|Keichō|ja|慶長|ko|게이초|ru|Кэйтё|simple|Keichō|sr|Кеичо|sv|Keichō|th|เคโช|tr|Keichō|uk|Кейтьо|zh|慶長|qid=Q1328185}} 4 ({{ill|1599|Q6803|qid=Q6803}}) and subsequently relocated to its present site<ref name="神々">“Gods of Japan,” entry on Nunakuma Shrine.</ref>.

There is also a theory that this Tomo Gion-gū corresponds to the “{{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Ekumi no Kunitsuyashiro}}” mentioned in fragments of the {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Bingo Province Fudoki}}<ref name="地名"/>. The shrine was revered as the tutelary deity of Tomo and received many donations from the lords of the Fukuyama Domain, owning shrine lands as well<ref name="地名"/>.

== Both shrines from the early modern period onward ==
The subsequent history of both shrines is as follows<ref name="神々"/>:
* During the Edo period, Tomo Gion-gū stood at this site, with Watasu Shrine as a subsidiary shrine within its precincts.
* In {{ill|Meiji era|Q3125096|qid=Q3125096}} 1 ({{ill|1868|ab|1868|af|1868|als|1868|am|1868 እ.ኤ.አ.|an|1868|ar|1868|ary|1868|arz|1868|ast|1868|avk|1868|az|1868|azb|۱۸۶۸ (میلادی)|ba|1868 йыл|ban|1868|bar|1868|bcl|1868|be|1868|be_x_old|1868|bg|1868|bn|১৮৬৮|bpy|মারি ১৮৬৮|br|1868|bs|1868.|ca|1868|cdo|1868 nièng|ce|1868 шо|ceb|1868|ckb|١٨٦٨|crh|1868|cs|1868|csb|1868|cv|1868|cy|1868|da|1868|de|1868|diq|1868|el|1868|eml|1868|eo|1868|es|1868|et|1868|eu|1868|fa|۱۸۶۸ (میلادی)|fi|1868|fiu_vro|1868|fo|1868|fr|1868|frp|1868|frr|1868|fur|1868|fy|1868|ga|1868|gan|1868年|gcr|1868|gd|1868|gl|1868|gv|1868|hak|1868-ngièn|he|1868|hi|१८६८|hif|1868|hr|1868.|hsb|1868|ht|1868 (almanak gregoryen)|hu|1868|hy|1868|hyw|1868 թուական|ia|1868|id|1868|ilo|1868|io|1868|is|1868|it|1868|ja|1868年|jv|1868|ka|1868|kaa|1868|kk|1868 жыл|kn|೧೮೬೮|ko|1868년|krc|1868 джыл|ku|1868|kv|1868-ӧд во|la|1868|lb|1868|lez|1868 йис|li|1868|lij|1868|lmo|1868|lt|1868 m.|lv|1868. gads|mai|१८६८|map_bms|1868|mdf|1868|mg|1868|mhr|1868|mi|1868|min|1868|mk|1868|ml|1868|mr|इ.स. १८६८|mrj|1868 и|ms|1868|my|၁၈၆၈|myv|1868 ие|mzn|۱۸۶۸|nah|1868|nap|1868|nds|1868|new|ई सं १८६८|nl|1868|nn|1868|no|1868|nrm|1868|nso|1868|oc|1868|olo|1868|or|୧୮୬୮|os|1868-æм аз|pa|1868|pap|1868|pl|1868|pnb|1868|pt|1868|qu|1868|ro|1868|roa_rup|1868|ru|1868 год|rue|1868|sa|१८६८|sah|1868|scn|1868|sco|1868|sd|1868ع|se|1868|sh|1868.|shn|1868|si|1868|simple|1868|sk|1868|sl|1868|smn|1868|sq|1868|sr|1868|stq|1868|su|1868|sv|1868|sw|1868|szl|1868|ta|1868|te|1868|tg|Соли 1868|th|พ.ศ. 2411|tk|1868|tl|1868|tly|1868|tr|1868|tt|1868 ел|udm|1868 ар|uk|1868|ur|1868ء|uz|1868|vec|1868|vi|1868|vls|1868|vo|1868|wa|1868|war|1868|wuu|1868年|xmf|1868|yi|1868|za|1868 nienz|zea|1868|zh|1868年|zh_classical|一八六八年|zh_min_nan|1868 nî|zh_yue|1868年|qid=Q7717}}), Tomo Gion-gū was renamed “Susanoo Shrine.”
* In Meiji 4 ({{ill|1871|Q7746|qid=Q7746}}), this Susanoo Shrine was designated as the Shikinaisha, renamed “Nunakuma Shrine,” and ranked as a {{ill|Q712534|lt=Kanpei-shōsha}} under the {{ill|Q712534|lt=Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines}}.
* In {{ill|1875|Q7764|qid=Q7764}} (Meiji 8) May, it was revised that Watasu Shrine was the Shikinaisha.
* In {{ill|1876|Q7766|qid=Q7766}} (Meiji 9) July, the spirit of Watasu Shrine was enshrined in the main hall, and the Gion deity was moved to an associated position (reversal of principal and subordinate). The Funadama deity of Watasu Shrine was reidentified as Ōwatatsumi-no-Mikoto.

== After World War II ==
* In {{ill|1957|Q5311|qid=Q5311}} (Shōwa 32) May, a main hall relocation ceremony was conducted. Offerings of ritual offerings and sacred food were presented by {{ill|Hirohito|Q34479|qid=Q34479}}<ref>{{Cite book |ja |author=Imperial Household Agency |title=The Shōwa Emperor’s Veritable Records, Vol. 12 |publisher=Tokyo Shoseki |date=2017-03-28 |page=327 |isbn=978-4-487-74412-1}}</ref>.

== Shrine precincts ==
[[File:Nunakuma-jinja shaden-2.jpg|thumb|220px|right|{{center|Shrine buildings}}]]
[[File:Nunakuma-jinja butai.JPG|thumb|220px|right|{{center|Noh stage (National {{ill|Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Q1188622|qid=Q1188622}})}}]]
The '''stone lanterns''' standing in front of the shrine buildings were donated in {{ill|Keian|Q1146135|qid=Q1146135}} 4 ({{ill|1651|Q6956|qid=Q6956}}) of the {{ill|Edo period|ar|فترة إيدو|ast|Periodu Edo|az|Edo dövrü|bcl|Panahon nin Edo|be|Перыяд Эда|bg|Едо (период)|bn|এদো যুগ|bo|ཨེ་དོའི་དུས་སྐབས།|br|Marevezh Edo|ca|Període Edo|ckb|سەردەمی ئێدۆ|cs|Období Edo|cv|Эдо тапхăрĕ|da|Edo-perioden|de|Edo-Zeit|eo|Epoko de Edo|es|Período Edo|et|Edo ajastu|eu|Edo aroa|fa|دوره ادو|fi|Edo-kausi|fr|Époque d'Edo|gl|Período Edo|he|תקופת אדו|hi|एदो अवधी|hr|Edo (razdoblje)|hu|Edo-kor|id|Zaman Edo|is|Jedótímabilið|it|Periodo Edo|ja|江戸時代|jv|Jaman Édo|ko|에도 시대|lt|Edo laikotarpis|lv|Edo periods|mk|Едо (период)|mn|Эдогийн эрин|ms|Zaman Edo|nl|Edoperiode|nn|Edotida|oc|Periòde Edo|pl|Edo (okres)|pt|Período Edo|ro|Perioada Edo|ru|Период Эдо|simple|Edo period|sk|Obdobie Edo|sl|Obdobje Edo|sq|Periudha Edo|sr|Едо период|su|Période Edo|sv|Edoperioden|th|ยุคเอโดะ|tl|Panahong Edo|tok|tenpo pi kulupu lawa Eto|tr|Edo Dönemi|uk|Період Едо|ur|ایڈو دور|uz|Edo davri|vi|Thời kỳ Edo|war|Panahon Edo|wuu|江戶時代|zh|江户时代|zh_min_nan|Edo sî-tāi|zh_yue|江戶時代|qid=Q184963}} by the third lord of the Fukuyama Domain, {{ill|Mizuno Katsusada|Q10565395|qid=Q10565395}}<ref name="石燈籠"/>. They stand 3.24 meters tall<ref name="石燈籠"/>. The large lanterns consist of a hexagonal base, a shaft stone 47.4 cm in diameter, and a middle platform, fire box, roof stone, and finial<ref name="石燈籠"/>. As exemplary shrine-front lanterns of the early modern period, they are designated Important Cultural Properties of Fukuyama City<ref name="石燈籠"/>.

Next to the Hachiman Shrine within the precincts are 20 '''chikara-ishi''' (strength stones). All are made of {{ill|Granite|af|Graniet|als|Granit|an|Granito|ang|Feldglæsstan|anp|ग्रेनाइट|ar|جرانيت|arz|جرانيت|ast|Granitu|az|Qranit|bar|Granit|be|Граніт|be_x_old|Граніт|bg|Гранит|bh|ग्रेनाइट|bn|গ্র্যানাইট|bpy|গ্রানিটো|br|Greunvaen|bs|Granit|ca|Granit|co|Granitu|cs|Žula|cy|Gwenithfaen|da|Granit|de|Granit|el|Γρανίτης|eo|Granito|es|Granito|et|Graniit|eu|Granito|ext|Granitu|fa|گرانیت|fi|Graniitti|fiu_vro|Graniit|fr|Granite|ga|Eibhear|gd|Eibhir|gl|Granito|gv|Clagh hryal|he|גרניט|hi|ग्रेनाइट|hr|Granit|hsb|Zornowc|ht|Granitik|hu|Gránit|hy|Գրանիտ|id|Granit|io|Granito|is|Granít|it|Granito|ja|花崗岩|ka|გრანიტი|kk|Гранит|kn|ಗ್ರಾನೈಟ್|ko|화강암|kw|Men growan|ky|Гранит|la|Granitum (lapis)|lb|Granit|lt|Granitas|lv|Granīts|mg|Vatorano|min|Granit|mk|Гранит|ml|കരിങ്കല്ല്|mn|Боржин|ms|Granit|mwl|Cantarie|my|နှမ်းဖတ်ကျောက်|mzn|گرانیت|nds|Granit|nl|Graniet|nn|Granitt|no|Granitt|oc|Granit|olo|Graniittu|os|Айнæгдур|pa|ਗਰੇਨਾਈਟ|pfl|Granit|pl|Granit|pnb|گرینائیٹ|ps|ګرانيټ ډبره|pt|Granito|qu|Alaymuska rumi|ro|Granit|ru|Гранит|sa|ग्रनैट् (शिला)|sh|Granit|simple|Granite|sk|Granit|sl|Granit|sq|Graniti|sr|Гранит|sv|Granit|sw|Itale|ta|கருங்கல் (பாறை)|tg|Хоро|th|หินแกรนิต|tr|Granit|tt|Гранит|uk|Граніт|uz|Granit|vi|Đá hoa cương|war|Granito|wuu|花岗岩|zh|花崗岩|zh_min_nan|Hoa-kong-gâm|zh_yue|麻石|qid=Q41177}}, oval in shape, and weigh between 118 and 230 kilograms<ref name="力石"/>. Each stone bears an inscription; five with known dates range from {{ill|Tenpō|Q1369045|qid=Q1369045}} 15 ({{ill|1844|Q7633|qid=Q7633}}) to {{ill|Ansei|cs|Ansei|de|Ansei|es|Ansei|fa|آنسی (دوره)|fr|Ère Ansei|ia|Ansei|it|Ansei|ja|安政|ko|안세이|ru|Ансэй|simple|Ansei|sr|Ансеи|sv|Ansei|tr|Ansei|zh|安政|qid=Q1327259}} 5 ({{ill|1858|Q7684|qid=Q7684}}). As Tomo was a maritime town, these stones are thought to have been offered in strength contests during festivals<ref name="力石"/>. Together with three stones at a nearby Sumiyoshi Shrine, they are designated as the “Tomo-no-Tsu Chikara-ishi,” Tangible Folk Cultural Properties of Fukuyama City<ref name="力石"/>.

One level below the main shrine buildings stands a Momoyama-period '''Noh stage'''. The structure is one bay by one bay, single-roofed, gabled, tsumairi style, with shingle roofing. It is said to have originally been a portable stage within {{ill|Fushimi Castle|Q1196273|qid=Q1196273}}, favored by {{ill|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|Q187550|qid=Q187550}}, and later granted by the second shogun {{ill|Tokugawa Hidetada|Q314464|qid=Q314464}} to {{ill|Mizuno Katsushige|Q8190277|qid=Q8190277}}, the first lord of the Fukuyama Domain, along with the Fushimi Yagura of Fukuyama Castle<ref name="説明板"/><ref name="能舞台"/>. During the {{ill|Manji (era)|Q1145295|qid=Q1145295}} era ({{ill|1658|Q6991|qid=Q6991}}–{{ill|1660|Q7001|qid=Q7001}}), the third lord {{ill|Mizuno Katsusada|Q10565395|qid=Q10565395}} donated it to the shrine, and in {{ill|Genbun|de|Genbun|fa|گنبون|fr|Ère Genbun|ja|元文|ko|겐분|ru|Гэмбун|simple|Genbun|sr|Генбун|sv|Genbun|tr|Genbun|zh|元文 (日本)|qid=Q1145754}} 3 ({{ill|1738|Q6996|qid=Q6996}}) it was converted into the fixed stage seen today<ref name="能舞台"/>. Features of its portable construction remain, with numbered markings on each component, indicating it could be transported even to battlefields<ref name="説明板"/>. The pine and bamboo painted on the kagami-ita (mirror board) date from the original period<ref name="能舞台"/>. The present bridge and dressing rooms, however, are later additions<ref name="能舞台"/>. Due to its valuable Momoyama-period characteristics, the stage is designated a National Important Cultural Property<ref name="能舞台"/>.

The '''second torii gate''' at the lowest level of the precincts was donated in {{ill|Kan'ei|Q1192913|qid=Q1192913}} 2 ({{ill|1625|Q6826|qid=Q6826}}) by Mizuno Katsushige (later the second lord {{ill|Mizuno Katsutoshi|Q10565388|qid=Q10565388}}) upon the birth of his eldest son (later the third lord {{ill|Mizuno Katsusada|Q10565395|qid=Q10565395}}), praying for his health<ref name="鳥居"/>. Although it is of the common Myōjin torii type, the ends of the kasagi are rounded and upturned, and a torifusuma is added, giving it a distinctive form<ref name="鳥居"/>. The upturned ends resemble the “Hizen torii” style, which may relate to the inscription on the pillars reading “Carpenter: Nakajima Yahyōe of Hizen”<ref name="鳥居"/>. This torii is designated an Important Cultural Property of Hiroshima Prefecture<ref name="鳥居"/>.

== Special rituals ==
; Oyumi Shinji
: Held on the 2nd Sunday of February. A festival of the Hachiman Shrine, originally conducted on the 7th day of the lunar New Year<ref name="お弓"/>. Participants include one adult parent archer and one adult child archer, two male pages, and two young arrow retrievers<ref name="お弓"/>. After performing ancient rites, arrows are shot from the stage toward a target in front<ref name="お弓"/>. This ritual is said to have evolved from the {{ill|Hamaya|Q138804|qid=Q138804|lt=hamayumi}} used to ward off evil at the beginning of the year, and is designated an Intangible Folk Cultural Property of the city<ref name="お弓"/>.

; Otebi Shinji
: “Otebi Shinji.” Held on the eve of the 2nd Sunday of July. A purification rite associated with Tomo Gion-gū, preceding the mikoshi procession<ref name="お手火"/>. Formerly held on the 4th day of the lunar 6th month<ref name="お手火"/>. During the ritual, sacred fire is lit on a large torch placed at the Zuishin Gate, and this torch is carried to the worship hall over the course of an hour<ref name="お手火"/>. After the mikoshi is brought out and placed in the worship hall, the torch is paraded through the precincts and town to purify defilement<ref name="お手火"/>. This ritual is designated an Intangible Folk Cultural Property of the city<ref name="お手火"/>.

== Cultural properties ==
== Important Cultural Properties (national designation) ==
* Noh Stage (Structure) – Designated November 14, 1953 (Shōwa 28)<ref name="能舞台">{{National Cultural Properties Database|102|3147|Nunakuma Shrine Noh Stage}}<br />[http://www.pref.hiroshima.lg.jp/site/bunkazai/bunkazai-data-102010240.html Nunakuma Shrine Noh Stage] (Hiroshima Prefectural Board of Education).<br />[http://www.city.fukuyama.hiroshima.jp/soshiki/bunka/5155.html Nunakuma Shrine Noh Stage] (Fukuyama City website).</ref>.

== Hiroshima Prefecture–designated cultural properties ==
* Important Cultural Property (Tangible Cultural Property)
** Torii Gate (Structure) – Early Edo period, built in Kan’ei 2 (1625). Designated February 5, 1957 (Shōwa 32)<ref name="鳥居">[http://www.pref.hiroshima.lg.jp/site/bunkazai/bunkazai-data-202010110.html Nunakuma Shrine Torii] (Hiroshima Prefectural Board of Education).<br />[http://www.city.fukuyama.hiroshima.jp/soshiki/bunka/5156.html Nunakuma Shrine Torii] (Fukuyama City website).</ref>.

== Fukuyama City–designated cultural properties ==
* Important Cultural Property (Tangible Cultural Property)
** Pair of Stone Lanterns (Structure)
**: Early Edo period, built in Keian 4 (1651). Designated January 31, 1967 (Shōwa 42)<ref name="石燈籠">[http://www.city.fukuyama.hiroshima.jp/soshiki/bunka/5143.html Nunakuma Shrine Stone Lanterns] (Fukuyama City website).</ref>.
** Noh Masks and Boxes (Crafts)
**: All from the Momoyama period and donated by {{ill|Mizuno Katsushige|Q8190277|qid=Q8190277}}, the first lord of the Fukuyama Domain. They are said to have originally been prized items of Toyotomi Hideyoshi, received by Katsunari from Tokugawa Hidetada together with the Noh stage. The Okina mask measures 19.39 cm in height and 16.06 cm in width, showing Momoyama-period stylistic features. The mask box is a reused item, decorated with gold maki-e on black lacquer depicting Ming-dynasty Chinese genre scenes. The outer box was made to preserve the mask box; an ink inscription inside the lid indicates it was prepared in {{ill|Eiroku|Q1143341|qid=Q1143341}} 8 ({{ill|1565|Q6634|qid=Q6634}}) by the Nakasuga family, hereditary shrine priests. Designated January 31, 1967 (Shōwa 42)<ref>[http://www.city.fukuyama.hiroshima.jp/soshiki/bunka/5228.html Noh Masks and Boxes] (Fukuyama City website).</ref>.
** Chigusa-made Kagura Tube (Craft)
**: Donated in {{ill|Manji (era)|Q1145295|qid=Q1145295}} 3 ({{ill|1660|Q7001|qid=Q7001}}) by {{ill|Mizuno Katsusada|Q10565395|qid=Q10565395}}, the third lord of the Fukuyama Domain, together with the Noh stage. The maker, Chigusa, was a Muromachi-period Noh mask carver. The tube is made of paulownia wood with black lacquer and gold maki-e phoenix designs. Designated January 31, 1967 (Shōwa 42)<ref>[http://www.city.fukuyama.hiroshima.jp/soshiki/bunka/5227.html Chigusa-made Kagura Tube] (Fukuyama City website).</ref>.
* Tangible Folk Cultural Property
** Tomo-no-Tsu Strength Stones – Designated together with 3 stones from Sumiyoshi Shrine. Designated September 22, 2000 (Heisei 12)<ref name="力石">[http://www.city.fukuyama.hiroshima.jp/soshiki/bunka/5271.html Tomo-no-Tsu Strength Stones] (Fukuyama City website).</ref>.
* Intangible Folk Cultural Property
** Oyumi Shinji – Designated March 31, 1971 (Shōwa 46)<ref name="お弓">[http://www.city.fukuyama.hiroshima.jp/soshiki/bunka/5264.html Oyumi Shinji] (Fukuyama City website).</ref>.
** Otebi Shinji – Designated March 31, 1973 (Shōwa 48)<ref name="お手火">[http://www.city.fukuyama.hiroshima.jp/soshiki/bunka/5265.html Otebi Shinji] (Fukuyama City website).</ref>.
